speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DECLARATION OP LOYALTY ON CELEBRATION OF BIRTHDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this being the day that has been designated to be celebrated as the birthday of Her Majesty Elizabeth II, Queen of Canada, I hope the Acting Leader of the Opposition will join with me in conveying congratulations from the House of Commons to Her Majesty. At the same time I know I speak for all Canadians when I say that she enjoys the loyalty and affection of all of us. After we have heard from opposition members, shall we then rise and join in summarizing our feelings by the singing of, "God Save the Queen"?
(Translation):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to say a few words in French, a language which has always been not only understood but very correctly spoken by our sovereigns.
I wish to associate myself with the words of congratulations which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has just addressed to Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II.
I should also like to express, if I may, the feelings of devotion, affection, attachment and loyalty of Canadians of French origin for Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II. History shows, Mr. Speaker, that in times of emergency the people of French Canada have always supported the British crown. Indeed, on one occasion, if not two, they took up arms against invaders of our Canadian territory.
It seems to me fitting that, on this day, a French voice be heard so as to echo from this side of the house the feelings that the Prime Minister has just expressed towards the gracious lady who, by virtue of the Statute of Westminster, is now Queen of Canada. Therefore, on behalf of the members of the opposition, I wish to make known to this house our feelings of affection and devotion to the Canadian crown.

subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON DISCUSSIONS IN NEW YORK

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minisier of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: TABLING OF REPORT ON DISCUSSIONS IN NEW YORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house I should like to table the report of the United Nations conference on lead and zinc.
In my statement to the house in advance of the conference on April 24 I explained that the Canadian government's views regarding the U.S. import quotas remained unchanged, and also that it would be made clear that Canada would be willing to explore the necessity for and possibility of an intergovernmental agreement for lead and zinc but that to be acceptable to Canada any such agreement must find wide support with all major importing and exporting countries playing their full part. I also referred to the representations which had been received from Canadian industry which has sought to avoid the necessity for an intergovernmental agreement and the regulation of exports, and the effects on mine production that such an agreement might entail.
As will be seen from the report which is being tabled, there was every indication prior to the conference that again in 1959 there

Tabling of Report on Lead and Zinc would be a substantial addition to world surplus stocks of lead and zinc as a result of the high level of production which was being maintained in the face of weakened and restricted markets. This situation could not, of course, continue indefinitely.
Shortly before the conference reports were received of decisions taken by private producers in one or two countries to reduce their production. These indications of a change of direction in production policies were noted by the conference and encouraged a broad reassessment of expectations on the part of the different delegations including their industry advisers. In a good number of cases this led to announcements dining the course of the conference of the intentions of other producers to curtail their production. In other cases governments, including that of the U.S.S.R., announced reductions in their expected or intended exports.
Hon. members will recall that the effect of the U. S. import quotas has been to restrict shipments by Canadian producers to the large United States market, and it became necessary for some of them to adjust production. The net effect of reduction by a number of our producers and revisions of previous forecasts is that Canadian exports will likely fall below 1958 levels by 9,000 tons of lead and 30,000 tons of zinc, as is indicated in the report.
If the revised forecasts are realized the annual rate of world production of zinc will be brought nearly into balance with expected consumption. Reduction from a forecast 120,000 ton surplus to a mere 16,000 tons for the world industry as a whole would be a major advance toward the restoration of more normal market conditions for zinc. The effect of forecast reductions in the case of lead is not quite so satisfactory, though there too the progress anticipated is significant.
I would not like to convey too optimistic an impression. The United States quota restrictions still remain in effect. Moreover, it should be noted that the report of the conference does not deal with the difficult problem of existing surplus stocks. However, it appears possible that as a result of voluntary decisions taken by private producers to adjust production to demand, the lead and zinc industries may have taken the first step on the way out of their recent difficulties.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RUSSIAN MESSAGE RESPECTING HIGH ALTITUDE NUCLEAR TESTS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON RUSSIAN MESSAGE RESPECTING HIGH ALTITUDE NUCLEAR TESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Would the Prime Minister comment on Mr. Khrushchev's latest message to President Eisenhower and Prime Minister Macmillan which appears to indicate the Soviet government's willingness to take part in a technical conference to study scientific information related to the detection of high altitude nuclear tests?
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, the reports in the press indicate that the Soviet appear to have taken a cautious step toward the solution of the problem of discontinuing nuclear tests. However, it would be a mistake to regard the expression of Mr. Khrushchev's views in an optimistic light, or to come to the conclusion that what has been said by him represents a concession of major significance. The house will recall that the question of detecting high 
altitude tests was discussed at length last summer at Geneva between western and Soviet experts, but those discussions were not pursued to agreed conclusions. Mr. Khrushchev's latest message, therefore, rather than initiating a fresh subject for negotiation represents merely an expression of renewed willingness to discuss an aspect of the problem on which a considerable amount of preparatory work has already been done.
It will be noted that his message is silent on the related question of how to detect subterranean tests. The aim with regard to subterranean tests is to reach agreement on a satisfactory number of annual inspections. On this aspect of the problem there was no encouragement whatsoever in Mr. Khrushchev's message as reported in the press.
All I can say is that while what has been suggested by him does represent at least a step forward, there is nothing in that statement which would lead the free world to believe that a major change of policy has been effected.

Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in asking the

Minister of Trade and Commerce a question. As the result of the recent meeting of representatives of Canada, the United States, Australia, France and Argentina in Washington to discuss the distribution of the world's No. 1 surplus food, namely wheat, to hungry people, is the Canadian government now giving consideration to accepting payment from the recipient countries in so-called soft currencies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: INQUIRY AS TO ACCEPTANCE OF PAY- MENT IN SOFT CURRENCIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have equal pleasure in replying to the hon. gentleman. He gave me notice of his question, which I think is based on a newspaper report that emanated from Washington. But in answer to the question, the policy of the government and of the wheat board is the same as it was last year, that is not to accept soft currency. During the last crop year 90 per cent of our export wheat was sold for cash. The remainder was disposed of either by way of loans on a three-year basis to, for example, Poland and Israel, or on long term loans to countries under the Colombo plan, or by way of outright gift to the Colombo plan countries. In the latter instance counterpart funds are set up for those outright gifts, that is, local currency; and those counterpart funds are used by the recipient country of the wheat to promote development projects within their own countries. We have no intention of changing that policy at the present time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Is the minister going to make a statement on this bill at this time?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill, which is known as Bill C-38, to reduce class and commodity rates on freight traffic, comes to the house as the minister has just said after examination by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. In that committee representations were heard from various groups indicating to the committee and to the government what their views were on the bill. I would have thought that in the light of those representations, sir, the Minister of Transport would have seen fit to indicate to the house what his views, those of his department and those of the government were in regard to those representations. It seems to me too, sir, that the minister should have given the house some indication, particularly in the light of the announcement made by the Prime Minister the other evening, on the royal commission on transportation. Unfortunately he has not seen fit to do this, and this prompts me to make a few observations on the bill as it comes from committee.
In the first place, out of the evidence that was given before the committee there comes some pertinent information having to do with this subsidy of $20 million which is being granted by parliament to various regions of Canada. One of those pertinent facts is the evidence given by one of the members of the board of transport commissioners to the effect that this subsidy will be divided among the various regions as follows: to the

Freight Rates
western region, 57.6 per cent, or $11,340,000; to the central region, 26.5 per cent or $5,300,000; and to the maritime region, 16.8 per cent or $3,360,000. Having regard to the fact that it was announced in this house that this was a measure to bring relief to the long haul provinces, it seems to me that here is positive proof and positive evidence that this measure will not provide relief to the long haul provinces as was anticipated.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to make a correction. I do not think it was ever said by me or by anybody on this side of the house that this was intended to relieve the long haul provinces; it was intended to relieve the long haul shippers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, I have not before me the statement made by the minister and that made by the Prime Minister, but there is no doubt in my mind what the implication of this measure is, that it is to come to the assistance of those who live in the far away parts of Canada, so the effect of the 17 per cent increase will be minimized to the extent of $20 million. That was clearly made the subject of statements made in this house.
However, the point I want to pursue is this; that had the committee been given the information which was asked, namely what was understood by a long and short haul and to what extent was the relief granted in the ten blocks established by the board of transport commissioners, then I am sure we would be able to ascertain and establish that the benefit of this subsidy is not nearly as great as was indicated and anticipated in favour of the long haul provinces. Unfortunately this information was not given. It is true that I did receive from the commissioner ten sheets, which were an analysis of the way bill sample, outlining the movements originating in one province and remaining in that province, but this information does not throw a great deal of light on the bill now before the house.
There is, however, another matter which I would like to discuss, sir, in relation to this measure, and that is the terms and the scope of the royal commission which was announced by the Prime Minister on Wednesday last. I would like to take this opportunity of saying, notwithstanding the statement which was made on that occasion, that the terms and the scope of the royal commission in my opinion are inadequate to deal with the problem that is now before us.
In the first place, before we consider that matter I think we must give some consideration to the reason the royal commission was established. The royal commission was

established because of the decision of the board of transport commissioners in November, 1958 authorizing a 17 per cent increase in freight rates to meet the wage increase which had been agreed upon between the railways and their employees. As the house knows, the provinces appealed this decision and the cabinet, in disallowing the appeal, stated that it would bring in a measure to relieve the inadequacies or inequities of the freight rate structure, and at the same time indicated that there would be a further study of the whole transportation problem in Canada.
The contention of the opposition at that time was that the government should have disposed of this problem earlier. The contention of the opposition was that in November, 1957 there was clear indication of this dispute between the railways and their employees, and if the government had then given the consideration which it should have given to this important matter then perhaps it would not have been necessary to take the action which was taken by the government, not of establishing the royal commission but of disallowing the appeal.
The wage increases for the employees, arose in November, 1957. It arose one year earlier than the statement made by the Acting Prime Minister, and it arose when the board of transport commissioners, faced with an application for an increase in freight rates because of an anticipated wage increase which at that time had not been agreed upon between the railways and the employees, had to make a determination of the issue, and the matter then came before the cabinet following the appeal from that decision. During the whole period of the wage negota-tions the government was aware that ultimately they would be called upon to give some consideration to the question and to take some positive action in order to settle the matter; but nothing was done and the matter was allowed to drift until the government was face to face with the appeal from the provinces.
I say, sir, that in my opinion the terms of this royal commission are inadequate. Before I give positive reasons for that assertion I should like to consider briefly the background. Why did the provinces appeal the decision? Though I was not present when the appeal was argued, I presume that one of the many reasons the provinces appealed the decision was that the long haul provinces suffered economic disadvantages on account of the long haul to markets and from the sources of supply which placed the Atlantic provinces and the western provinces in particular at a relative disadvantage in reaching

central Canadian markets in competition with producers in other parts of Canada, and particularly with producers who had shorter hauls to make.
The maritime provinces take the view that the Maritime Freight Rates Act should be retained and extended, and they want, to a large degree, the equalization of freight rates. The prairie provinces want the retention of the Crowsnest rates, and they too demand equalization of freight rates. They also would like closer supervision over the establishment of competitive rates. British Columbia wants the preservation of its transcontinental rates together with a greater equalization of freight rates.
In effect	this	means that	the	provinceswant lower freight rates, although different methods are suggested; some provinces favour one method, whereas other provinces favour another. Whatever method is suggested as the solution to this important problem, the object will be the same, namely to give to the shipper and to the consignee greater relief from the disadvantages attributed to	the	increases in	rates by the
horizontal percentage method, and at the same time to retain any existing advantages in rates which are enjoyed by the shipper and the consumer.
On the other hand, the railways want the preservation of the horizontal rate increases; they say that is their method of obtaining relief from	the	increasing costs	of transportation in	this	country.
Therein lies the clash between the provinces, on the one hand, and the railways on the other. It seems that between these two points of view a solution must be found. The royal commission has been established with the object in view, I presume, of finding some relief from that problem. What do the terms of the royal commission do in order to meet this point? Nothing specific is stated in the terms of reference to this question I have just raised. I say that the terms are inadequate, first because there is no specific reference in the order in council to horizontal rate increases and to the effect these increases will have upon the long haul provinces.
I ask you, Mr. Chairman, to consider the attitude of the government when they sat on this side of the house, and how hon. gentlemen opposite rose in their places and inveighed against the impact of horizontal rate increases from one end of the country to another and, by implication, indicated that when they got into office they would do something to relieve that burden. I say there is no specific reference to this problem, which to me is one of the most serious problems-1
Freight Rates

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
What about subsection
(a)?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
-as indicated by the Prime
Minister and others when they sat on this side of the house. In a moment, if I may, I shall deal with subsection (a) in connection with horizontal rate increases. Then I will ask the committee to consider the attitude adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite during the election campaign. Will the Prime Minister allow me to read to him what he said on May 18, 1957 at Drumheller. He stated on that occasion:
-there should be equalization of rail rates in Canada "within reasonable limits" to give a shot in the arm to agriculture and industry on the prairies.
He is reported a little further on as having said:
-that a rate pattern discriminatory to the west has been made worse by recent increases. This had struck "an almost paralyzing blow" to industrial development in the west.
And still later, according to a report in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 20, 1957, he is reported as having said:
-a Conservative government would equalize freight rates as far as possible to help both agriculture and industry on the prairies compete with the rest of Canada.
When these statements were made there had been three reports submitted by the board of transport commissioners equalizing freight rates to the extent that they could be equalized at the time. One of these reports is dated May 25, 1955.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean by the words "to the extent that they could be equalized at the time"?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I mean this, that freight rates were equalized in western Canada. I mean, further, that freight rates were equalized on a long list of commodities as set out in Mr. Justice Kearney's report dated March 25, 1955 of which, I am sure, the Prime Minister could not have taken cognizance when he made the statement he did. I mean, also, the report on equalization dated September 22, 1957. This is the one handed down by chief commissioner Clarence Shepard in which is detailed a long list of class and commodity rates which had been equalized.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman suggest that these lists covered all the commodities which affect western Canada and the Atlantic provinces?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
I suggest this, that if the Prime Minister had read those three reports -and I know it is impossible for him to read everything which has to do with this

Freight Rates
subject-he would have amended the statement he made during the campaign, because these are three reports dealing clearly and without equivocation with what has been done by the board of transport commissioners to equalize freight rates in Canada. I think they are well worth reading, because they indicate to what extent the board has gone in dealing with this question of equalization.
1 return now to the terms of reference. It was suggested that term (a) of order in council P.C. 1957/577 covered the question I discussed earlier about the impact of horizontal freight rates. The point I was making was that this subsection does not deal particularly with the impact of horizontal freight rates, and having regard to the fact that members of the government when sitting on this side of the house complained so bitterly about this matter, it would seem to me that this was one of the first things they would have mentioned in the scope of the reference.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Is this not comprehensive enough to cover it?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
I doubt very much whether it is, because the words are so broad that they could probably mean anything. But having regard to the fact that certain charges were made it would have seemed to me that a particular reference could have been included to cover the matter.
May I now draw another point to the attention of the government. It is stated that the commissioners are appointed to inquire into and report upon certain problems, one of which is stated to be inequities in the freight rate structure, their incidence upon the various regions of Canada, etc. My suggestion is this. I doubt very much whether there are inequities in the freight rate structure in the sense mentioned here. What I am saying is that there are inequalities. I know the Prime Minister is ready to rise and blast at me because of that statement, but I shall repeat it. I doubt very much if there are inequities in the legal sense of the word. There may be inequalities in the freight rate structure and I think there probably are serious ones, but how could there be inequities in the sense in which this is meant when the Railway Act clearly says that the moment an application is made to the board of transport commissioners the board shall deal with the matter as it comes before them? I refer to section 328, subsection 5 of the Railway Act which states:
-the powers given to the board under this act to fix, determine and enforce just and reasonable rates, and to change and alter rates as changing conditions or cost of transportation may from time to time require, are not limited or in any manner affected by the provisions of any act of the parliament of Canada-

I submit that the freight rates which have been determined by the board of transport commissioners, while they may be unequal because of the vast distances in Canada, are not inequitable because they are authorized under statute passed by parliament. To that extent I say that the wording of this section is not sufficient in order to cover adequately the impact of the horizontal rate increases.
Furthermore, the scope of this inquiry is not adequate because it contains no specific reference to the problems of the Canadian National Railways. Is there any railway in Canada or on the North American continent which at this time is suffering greater difficulties because of lack of traffic and competition from other sources than the Canadian National Railways? It seems to me that with a deficit of $51 million for the year 1959 as announced by the president and an estimated deficit of $34 million for the year 1960, some specific reference should have been made in the scope of this inquiry to deal with the problems of the Canadian National Railways which are most urgent at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question, Mr. Chairman. Is the hon. member suggesting that the commission should have been given power to examine all the ramifications of the Canadian National Railways?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
I am not suggesting that, Mr. Chairman. What I am suggesting is that the commission might well have been given power to deal with what assistance could be given to help the C.N.R. in getting around its fixed charges. That is a matter that has come up in parliament from time to time and one about which the Canadian National Railways is greatly apprehensive. Without going into the whole scope of railway transportation I believe the government might well have given consideration to asking the commission to give specific attention to some of the problems of the Canadian National Railways that are most imminent at this time.
There is complete exclusion from this reference to the functions of the board of transport commissioners. I am not complaining about that, but I draw the attention of the government to the following fact. The Prime Minister will remember that when he and his associates sat on this side of the house they criticized the board of transport commissioners by saying that they were useless and were not doing their job properly. If that was the case, why did they not ask the commission to inquire into the functions of the board? Now that they sit on the other side of the chamber and see it in a different light they find that the board is operating

satisfactorily, or at least they do not intend to consider an inquiry into the board's functions.
Again, there is no specific reference to the problem referred to in the statement made by the acting prime minister in November of last year, namely the problem that in future the board of transport commissioners should not take it upon themselves to increase freight rates until a definite agreement had been made between the railway company and its employees on the subject of wages. There is no mention of that. This seemed to be a highly important matter when it came up for discussion and was contained in the statement made by the acting prime minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member for Laurier to explain in more detail what he means by this suggestion? What does he think should have been written into the terms of the commission in this respect?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the request of the Prime Minister the other evening I indicated what I thought should be considered by the royal commission. The Prime Minister rose and said in effect that if anybody in the chamber wanted to tell the government what it should give consideration to with reference to the terms of the royal commission they should make suggestions. I rose and made four suggestions. The Minister of Public Works now asks me what I have to suggest. I am saying that the minister was complaining about this position in which the board of transport commissioners found themselves in having to raise rates because wages had been increased. The minister then made the statement that he did not think the board should be put in that position. Why should not the scope of the inquiry extend to that matter? Why should not that matter be studied so that if in future a similar situation arises the board will know what to do? Under section 328, subsection 5, the board has no other alternative but to deal with applications which come before it as those applications are launched by the railway association of Canada.
Then there is the other matter to which the Prime Minister himself referred when he made the announcement of the royal commission. I should like to quote his words. If I interpret them wrongly I am sure he will correct me. At page 3607 of Hansard of May 13 the Prime Minister said:
When the Minister of Public Works as acting prime minister announced the government's intention to arrange for this review he assured the western farmers that such review would not mean that they would have to pay more freight on the shipment of grain for export. Surely there is nothing which would affect in any way the rights of people in western Canada if that were done. And if perchance it were found that the rates are not compensatory to the railways, then the royal commission might want to make a recommendation to parliament for the payment of a subsidy on behalf of the western farmer, who benefits from the movement of grain because of the Crowsnest rates, in the same manner

If that were a recommendation of the royal commission and the government decided to implement it, I am sure that parliament would give it the consideration which is required in these matters and which it would deserve under all conditions.
Here it seems to me that a study of the railway transportation problem in Canada, an inquiry so important to railway transportation in Canada, is not complete unless there is a study of this problem because it is one of the most serious problems that exist today, as the Prime Minister knows. It comes up in the committee from time to time; it comes up in the house and it seems, in my opinion at least, that some consideration should have been given to it.
There is no question of eliminating an agreement or changing the agreement that was enacted by parliament away back in 1897. There is no intention on the part of those who sit on this side of the house to affect or change that agreement in any way whatsoever. That has been made quite clear on many occasions. But it is the railways who find themselves in a difficult position. It seems to me it would be just giving the members of 
this commission an additional term of reference, an additional scope of the reference, in order to consider what is of tremendous importance to the economy of western Canada.
Then, sir, there is no specific reference to the one and one-third rule which affects the province of Alberta so much, the one and one-third rule which has been lost as regards agreed charges. Then it seems to me the inquiry ought not to have been limited in its scope as it has been. It seems to me the government has narrowed the scope of the inquiry by the terms which have been set out.
Then there was the very important statement made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport, that there is to be no increase in freight rates until the commission reports its findings. How long is the commission going to take? It seems to me that a most important task has been given to the members of the royal commission. If they are to do their jobs in the way parliament wants them to do them it may take more than a year. It took the Turgeon commission two and a half years. It is true this commission may do its work much faster. I am not saying that is not possible; but I am saying that future applications to the board of transport commissioners, future increases in freight rates, are tied down because of the statements which have been made. This is not an equitable way to deal with the commission which, it seems to me, should have all the time required to consider and report upon what is a most important problem.
Without trespassing unduly on the time of the committee I could go on with other matters, but I shall not do so. I will simply conclude by saying that the royal commission on transportation have a difficult and important task. Their duties are set out in the preamble to the order in council, which indicates that they are to inquire with reasonable dispatch into problems relating to railway transportation in Canada and the possibility of removing or alleviating inequities in the freight rate structure. With that statement no one can disagree. With the general and broad statement contained in the preamble to the order in council no one, I think, can find fault with it; but then, when it is broken down, it seems to me that there are specific problems having to do with transportation in Canada that should have been mentioned.
I mentioned four of them. On an earlier occasion I mentioned some of the matters which it seemed to me the railways were charged with, and consideration should be given to those matters. Whether the scope of this inquiry is broad enough to consider those I am not in a position to say, but I know that I would have felt a great deal happier, as

many hon. members in this house would have felt, if the terms had been spelled out in such a way that many other problems affecting railway transportation could have been considered in this inquiry.

happy and the railways kept as going concerns, is this: There has been a two-sided argument in so far as the Crowsnest pass rates and other freight subsidies are concerned, and they pit farmers in the west against railway labour. Management and other people argue that subsidization is outrageous, and subsidies such as we are putting through here are nothing but a sop to labour and on the other hand subsidies like the Crowsnest pass rates are nothing but a handout to the western farmers. I do not believe the prairie farmer can afford any increase in the charges on his wheat. I feel that if anything we should be thinking, not of an increase in the prairie rates but a decrease. The point in so far as railway labour is concerned is this: Every time they want an increase the western farmers get excited, with newspaper encouragement, and say that these are the people who are putting pressure upon the Crowsnest pass rates. I suggest that if the Canadian Pacific railway is the key to western grain rates, not the Canadian National Railways, and the Canadian Pacific must earn 4 per cent on their stock, then let us establish that through this commission. Then we could say that we will see this free enterprise organization is subsidized to the extent of the non-compensatory margin, but we are going to keep these grain rates as they are or, if necessary, reduce them. We are going to try to get away from the situation where every time the railway unions ask for more money hands are thrown up and people say it is coming directly out of the federal taxpayer's pocket. This is one of the reasons I hope this commission will go into the facts relating to the Crowsnest pass agreement. If one looks at the terms of reference, I believe the commission will be in a position to do so.
In other words, let us find out how much the Canadian Pacific has made out of Consolidated Mining and Smelting over the years, and out of those properties given to them decades ago, from which they get gas and oil revenues. It seems to me that the real criticisms that can be made about this legislation are ones that have to do with the present mood and purposes of this government. It is in a very dull mood and the performance is not one that gives any feeling of energetic leadership. The issue came up last November when the Minister of Public Works made his statement. Here it is May before we get the royal commission announced, and we certainly seem to have been dawdling through this freight rate problem. I do not mean dawdling in the house, but I mean in working out a system by means of which the $20 million is to be circulated throughout the whole freight rate structure.
The very figure of $20 million intrigues me. Why was it struck? It only reflects 7 per cent of the 17 per cent increase, but it seems to me that $20 million was the best bargain the Minister of Trade and Commerce could get out of the Minister of Finance. It seems to me that $20 million is probably the best bargain the Minister of Trade and Commerce could get out of the Minister of Finance. It seems to me a pity that he could not have obtained a little better bargain in terms for the freight shippers. As to the royal commission and where it is going to go, it is certainly apparent that its report is not going to be ready in time and that we are going to have to do something about putting something more through this complicated process. The fundamental question in transportation in this country still boils down to this. It has been said before and it needs to be said again. We must make up our minds, in so far as the railroad side of it is concerned, whether we are going to continue to hobble along between the principle of socialism or free enterprise or, if we want to put it another way, whether we are going to recognize outright that transportation is, in the public domain, a public utility and that therefore the ordinary business costs and business efficiency that would apply to an enterprise in the private sector do not apply here. I can certainly agree with the feelings of Mr. Crump as expressed in his annual reports over the last few years with regard to the frustration of a private corporation trying to do business under the limitations under which the C.P.R. operate. To me and to the people in this group the solution is for us to move logically to the position that this is a field of public enterprise, not of private enterprise, and that until we move in that way we are going to have to continue to have this bastard arrangement of private enterprise and public enterprise, with the advocates of each condemning the other, and no real knowledge about where we are going.

Mr. Chairman, coming from the most easterly province in Canada and an island province I am naturally keenly interested in anything that has to do with freight rates. The cost of freight is vital to the economy of my constituency as indeed it is to the entire province of Newfoundland. Practically all of our consumer goods have to be imported including clothing, food, much of our building material and indeed most of the necessities of life. These are brought in by rail and ship. The products of our mines and our fisheries as well as our pulp and paper products have to be exported. The cost of moving goods in and out can mean the difference between solvency and bankruptcy

for people in this area. While this bill will give some help it will not give sufficient assistance considering the extent of the disability of the Atlantic provinces and particularly of Newfoundland.
The position of Newfoundland was very well stated by Mr. Edgar Miller, a prominent Newfoundland businessman, writing in the Daily News when he said:
Once more Newfoundland will bear far more than its fair share of this new freight increase. The 17 per cent has been applied as a percentage to existing tolls. We are at the end of the line and we pay the highest rates, so it is inevitable that we must contribute the greatest part to this increased freight cost.
-we are the people in Canada who are least able to afford to carry the burden of the railway's additional cost of operations. Here in Newfoundland we literally have no competitive rates or agreed charges.
-each year our contribution to the railway's increased cost for operation has been larger than each preceding year. A recent study disclosed that between 70 per cent and 80 per cent of the traffic in the Atlantic provinces-possibly higher in Newfoundland-moves on non-competitive rates and so all of this will be increased by 17 per cent.
While the Maritime Freight Rates Act does provide some benefits it is of the least importance to us. Practically all of our exports move by water and these are not eligible for the subventions. Except for a few competitive rates on traffic originating east of Montreal during the summer months, we have no competitive rates. Being at the end of the line our rates are the highest. Consequently all of our in-bound traffic, representing the necessities of life, will be subjected to the full impact of this latest freight rate increase. I suggest this province, its industries and its people are less able to supDort the railway than the rest of Canada.
May I suggest that transportation is a national family concern, yet under the present system those provinces that are not as well able to bear increased costs are required to shoulder them. May I point out that what I shall refer to as the centre of Canada sells to Newfoundland about $250 million worth of goods a year. As a matter of fact, the province of Newfoundland is the third greatest overseas market of Canada and I refer to it in those terms because Newfoundland is an island. Newfoundland buys more from the rest of Canada than does any market other than the United States and the United Kingdom.
With all due deference I should also like to point out that Canada sends millions of dollars worth of goods to Ghana and other countries which she justifiably hopes will develop and become customers. Is it not just as important or possibly more important to look after the interests of one who is already a good customer? All we are asking for is equality of opportunity. I should like to pass on a suggestion which has been made

that in considering the position of the mari-times and Newfoundland consideration might be given to a roll back of rates to 1948 plus an increase based on a constant dollar.
In closing I should like to make a purely personal observation. From my limited knowledge of freight rates it seems they are getting more complicated every year. As a matter of fact there is some excuse for thinking that the best minds in Canada are spending their time making them more intricate as time goes on. This leads one to suspect that, given time, no doubt there will be one freight rate applicable to rice krispies and another applicable to sugarpops. I should like to suggest that some consideration be given to the possibility, remote though it may be, of applying the principle of the postage stamp to freight rates; that is, simplify the structure so that it would cost the same amount to move a pound of freight anywhere in Canada regardless of the distance involved.

We have this royal commission which has been set up. It has, I think, very substantial powers to inquire into the effect of freight rates. I believe its terms of reference, so far as freight rates themselves are concerned, are very comprehensive. For example, paragraph (d) says that the commission shall

consider and report upon whether, and to what extent, the Railway Act should specify what assets and earnings or railway companies in businesses and investments other than railways should be taken into account in establishing freight rates. I think that is one of the most important terms of reference because, in the past, we have had the Canadian Pacific used as the yardstick. The board of transport commissioners, in determining the level of freight rates, has allowed the Canadian Pacific, in its accounting statements, to set aside those enterprises from which it has made very substantial profits and to consider its railway operations only. I do not believe such a division is fair or just. I believe that the Canadian Pacific's total position as a company should be considered whenever it asks for a freight rate increase.
I make that statement precisely because of these tremendous land grants and cash grants over the years which have been used by the Canadian Pacific to extend its operations into the field of air lines, hotel services, into the smelting business, into the petroleum business, and many other activities which have produced revenue for the Canadian Pacific.
I have been asked a question earlier, Mr. Chairman, as to my attitude about the 17 per cent increase in freight rates. I have said that it was my opinion the government should not have allowed this increase to take place. The inference is left that every time the railway workers get an increase in wages this automatically must result in an increase in freight rates. This is a premise I do not accept. I think the railway companies have shown over recent years a very great ability to reduce the number of workers necessary to operate the railways. One has only to refer to the size of freight trains to illustrate the very substantial reduction in labour as compared with freight trains in the early years. Freight trains used to have 30 or 40 box cars, but today's freight trains are often in excess of 100 railway cars and are operated by the same number of persons.
The program of dieselization has brought about very large savings to the railway companies. Earlier I mentioned Mr. MacPherson. I might say that in his statement to the board of transport commissioners on October 31, 1957 he pointed out that the evidence given by the Canadian Pacific vice-president, Mr. Emerson, shows that, comparing 1947 with 1957, there was a saving from dieselization alone of $45 million on an expenditure of $138 million. Mr. MacPherson points out that at that time the railways had been dieselized only to the extent of 48 per cent, 72 per cent passenger and 68 per cent yard. The railways
[Mr. Argued
in Canada must have made further, substantial savings in the intervening time as a result of dieselization.
The modernization of railways would dispense with much of the labour that has been used in the past. I understand that when the president of the Canadian National, Donald Gordon, was before a committee of this house he said in reply to a question that he could foresee the time when freight trains in this country would be operating without any people on the trains, completely automatic freight trains. If we had completely automatic freight trains in this country, do hon. members think that, without persons operating on freight trains, the railways would decide they needed no further increases in freight rates because they would not then be able to put the blame on increases in wages?
Of course, so long as cost increases continue, and so long as the railways are desirous of earning a substantial profit, we will be faced with further demands for increases in freight rates. We do not feel that this royal commission has been necessary, but we do admit that the personnel of the commission gives us some hope that the recommendations may be improved, and that if they are, and if the government acts, then the continued horizontal increases in freight rates may be halted. We may then have a more equitable freight rate system in this country, and our railways may provide again the national service that is expected from them. Then, too, the workers of this industry would not be discriminated against but would have an opportunity to improve their standard of living as Canadians in other occupations are able to do from time to time.

This bill which is entitled "an act to make provision for the reduction of certain class and commodity rates on freight traffic" is of vital importance to my province; and to the extent that it will achieve this purpose, we welcome it and support it.
We in Newfoundland have the highest cost of living in all of Canada, and the most important factor in that high cost of living is freight rates. We know that this legislation is consequent upon an increase of 17 per cent in freight rates. It has been estimated that this subsidy will, in its effect, reduce that increase to 10 per cent. I think we must realize that these figures are only theoretical. They would be true if the same factors applied all across Canada, but that is not the case. The figure of 17 per cent is artificially high because in the central provinces other factors such as truck competition and water competition make it impossible to benefit from that increase to any extent. The burden of the extra revenue must

therefore come from the Atlantic provinces and from the western provinces. It is, of course, for that reason that the two central provinces do not even bother to appear before the board of transport commissioners and oppose these freight rate increases because they know an increase is not going to affect them materially in any way at all.
We had hoped that the distribution of this subsidy of $20 million would be carried out in such a way as to offset, as much as possible, these inequalities in the freight rates and in the freight structure owing to the factors which obtain in the central provinces and which are not operative in the eastern and western provinces.
If my understanding of clause 3 is correct, this subsidy will apply only to commodities where the full 17 per cent goes into effect. If that is not the case, I hope the minister will correct me when he replies. I think perhaps that is an advantage to the western provinces and to the Atlantic provinces because certainly they are going to have the greatest percentage of traffic upon which the full 17 per cent increase will be applied. But the figures which my friend the hon. member for Laurier put on the record just now, if they are even approximately correct, would suggest that the inequality is still going to exist to a remarkable degree. The central region is going to get 26.5 per cent of the $20 million or $5,300,000 while the maritime region will get 16.8 per cent or a total of $3,316,000.
The point I want to make is this. For traffic in the central provinces where the full 17 per cent increase is applied, that full subsidy goes into effect and will reduce it down to 10 per cent, which figure perhaps would be much lower than would otherwise be the case if just the normal competitive factors were allowed to operate. I am not going to complain about that fact. I think it should put the railway in a much better competitive position vis-a-vis the trucking industry and water transportation and should perhaps result in increased traffic and increased revenue for the railways so that a greater part of that $5 million which the central region is going to get may be recovered from them. If that is the case, the total subsidy would be reduced only to about, say, $15 million.
The maritimes, of course, are going to get an extremely small share of this subsidy and Newfoundland will get the least of all. As the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador pointed out just now, the products of our industries are shipped direct from Newfoundland to foreign markets. We are in a much different position from that of the other maritime provinces. Mainland Canada
Freight Rates
buys very little from us. As to the paper that is shipped direct from Corner Brook or from Botwood to the British or the United States markets, I cannot see how it is going to get benefit as a result of this subsidy. The fish products that are shipped direct from the various cold storage plants are not going to benefit by it. This subsidy will not benefit our industries at all. Hence the benefit we get out of this subsidy is going to be derived mainly from the things that we buy from the mainland. Our total traffic in that respect is going to be in smaller proportion than that of the other maritime provinces.
I was greatly interested in what the minister said about this subsidy being passed on to the consumer. I know that the trouble with subsidies is that they seldom benefit the people we really want to help. I must confess that I find it extremely difficult to believe that the consumer in Newfoundland will benefit very much or even at all from this subsidy. If the government increases a tax, we know that immediately the prices go up in much greater proportion than does the tax itself. But when taxes are reduced, it is seldom that the full reduction is passed on to the consumer. The various people who handle the product always find some way of absorbing it. Suppose a merchant in some outport in Newfoundland, has on his shop shelves a shipment of tinned fruit which he now sells for 25 cents a tin, and gets in another shipment on which the freight charges are slightly less because of this subsidy. I cannot visualize that he is going to cut his price down from 25 cents to 23 cents. I find it difficult to visualize such a thing happening. I just wonder whether the minister had in mind any way by which the interests of the consumer could be safeguarded so that we could make sure that he would benefit from this subsidy.
Apart from that, I hope that we can find a better way of distributing subsidies of this kind than we have had up to date and even better than the one we have in this bill although I admit, by confining it to commodities which bear the full rate of the increase, it is perhaps fairer to the maritimes and the eastern provinces than would be the case if it were just a straight reduction.
That is all I have to say, Mr. Chairman, but this point of safeguarding the interests of the consumer is very much in my mind and I would like the minister, when he replies, to say if he has any ideas of enforcing my suggestion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND OPERATION, APPOINTMENT OF MEMBERS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this proposal to establish a national energy board which we have before us for consideration is the fulfilment of an objective held by the Conservative party over the years. That objective was clearly stated on February 25, 1955, at page 1530 of Hansard by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, now Minister of Public Works, in the following words:
We believe there is a great need for an over-all energy policy. Let us get away from dealing with the problem piecemeal with different departments concerned. It is not an efficient way to deal with

these important matters. For example, we suggest that consideration be given to setting up what might be called a national energy board under which could be gathered a professional staff to deal with those questions which would have the necessary information and the necessary training and which could recommend policy to the government. Then, once policy had been decided by the government, the board could implement that policy.
We believe the energy resources are among Canada's greatest assets, and that they can go far to make her one of the leading nations of the world. But if this is to be done we must get away from the present hit and miss method of dealing with those resources. We must have in Canada a national energy policy for the use of those resources, and the administrative machinery to carry it out.
When the opportunity arrived for the present government to take steps toward developing the policy outlined above an order in council was passed on October 15, 1957 setting up a royal commission on energy. The preamble of that order reads in part as follows:
That inasmuch as Canada has within its boundaries large sources of energy in the form of gas, oil, coal, water and uranium, the increasing need of energy for the growing industrial requirements of Canada renders it of the greatest importance to assure the most effective use of those resources in the public interest;
That it is desirable that an investigation be made now into a number of questions relating to sources of energy in order to assist in determining the principles and procedures to be applied in the administration of certain aspects of energy policy which fall within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada;
The royal commission was instructed to inquire into and make recommendations concerning, among other matters:
(a)	the policies which will best serve the national interest in relation to the export of energy and sources of energy from Canada;
(b)	the problems involved in, and the policies which ought to be applied to, the regulation of the transmission of oil and natural gas between provinces or from Canada to another country including, but without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the regulation of prices or rates to be charged or paid, the financial structure and control of pipe-line corporations in relation to the setting of proper prices or charges, and all such other matters as it is necessary to inquire into and report upon, in order to ensure the efficient and economical operation of pipe lines in the national interest:
(c)	the extent of authority that might best be conferred on a national energy board to administer, subject to the control and authority of parliament, such aspects of energy policy coming within the jurisdiction of parliament as it may be desirable to entrust to such a board, together with the character of administration and procedure that might best be established for such a board;
The members of the royal commission were Henry Borden, Esq., C.M.G., Q.C. of the city of Toronto, Chairman; J. Louis Levesque, Esq., of the city of Montreal; George Edwin Britnell, Esq., of the city of Saskatoon; Gordon G. Cushing, Esq., of the city of Ottawa; Robert

D. Howland, Esq., of the city of Halifax, and Leon J. Ladner, Esq., Q.C., of the city of Vancouver.
Subsequently, Dr. R. M. Hardy of the University of Alberta was appointed to the commission, and Mr. Cushing resigned to become assistant deputy minister of the Department of Labour.
The commission held public hearings in Victoria, Calgary, Regina, Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal, in the course of which it has taken some 8,500 pages of evidence and received about ninety submissions.
In October, 1958 the commission submitted a first report dealing with some aspects of its inquiry and will submit a second report soon concerning some specific problems relating to crude oil.
Since receiving the report the government has studied it very carefully. Detailed and constructive comment upon the report has been supplied by provincial governments, and by various segments of the industries concerned and by investment firms.
The commission deserves congratulations and thanks for the exhaustive study it has made of the matters before it and for the conscientious discharge of its heavy responsibilities. Many of its recommendations are to be implemented as will be clear when the bill is before the house.
The measure, as the resolution indicates, has as its principal purpose the establishment of a national energy board. It is proposed that this board have most of the powers now held by the board of transport commissioners under the Pipe Lines Act, and those parts of the Railway Act incorporated in the Pipe Lines Act by reference.
Whereas under the Pipe Lines Act the board of transport commissioners has power to grant or withhold leave to construct pipe lines under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, the new board in respect of applications for the construction of pipe lines would have the power to grant or withhold, subject to the approval of the governor in council, certificates of public convenience and necessity. It is proposed that the new measure supersede the Pipe Lines Act, and also the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act.
The new board would, on the basis of public hearings, and subject to the approval of the governor in council, grant or deny licences to export electric power or gas or to import gas.
The board would exercise certain broad advisory functions ranging over the whole field of energy and sources of energy in so far as the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction over such matters. The board would
National Energy Board have jurisdiction over tolls charged by all pipe-line companies subject to the act, and over prices at which gas and power might be exported.
The bill will set out, in much the same way as the present Pipe Lines Act, the general powers of pipe line companies subject to the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. The bill will contain provisions for transition from arrangements under the existing statutes to corresponding new arrangements.
These are the main elements of the proposed bill. I come now to certain points of policy which underlie the bill and which will guide the administration of the measure if approved by parliament.
We recognize the need for and welcome capital whether domestic or foreign for investment in the energy and associated industries, and we believe such capital, wisely invested, should enjoy a fair and reasonable rate of return. As to what is a fair return, it is not our intention to incorporate any fixed formula in the statute. Rather, our first premise is that returns on successful investment must be sufficient to attract capital for replacement and expansion, and our second premise is that the public interest requires that no pipe line company should exploit its monopoly or quasi-monopoly position to secure returns higher than are fair and reasonable. Certain general criteria will be set forth in the bill, and their application will be left to the fair and impartial judgment of the well-qualified men whose services on the board we hope to obtain.
We recognize that gas pipe lines are different from oil pipe lines, and that both are different from public utilities such as electric light and water service. Both oil and gas are subject to competition from other fuels and sources of energy, and an oil pipe line may be subject to competition in its markets by oil from other sources. There are elements of risk for both kinds of pipe line, and perhaps more risk for oil pipe lines than for gas pipe lines.
The customer of the gas pipe line is more nearly captive in that he cannot readily turn to another source of gas. The consumer of the gas in order to use an alternative fuel must convert his equipment or replace it if his gas supply becomes uneconomic or otherwise unsatisfactory. There is therefore a clear case for regulating the returns of gas pipe line companies.
The oil pipe line may not have the same sort of captive market. However, for some refineries one oil pipe line may be the only practical source of supply, and for many oil producers one oil pipe line is the only practical outlet to market. Therefore for practical

National Energy Board purposes an oil pipe line is a carrier in a monopoly or quasi-monopoly position, and should be regulated as such. For somewhat different reasons, therefore, we have come to the conclusion that the returns of both oil pipe lines and gas pipe lines should be regulated, though not necessarily on the same terms or at the same level.
While we have reached the conclusion that in the public interest there should be appropriate regulation of the returns of gas and oil pipe line companies, it is not the intention of the government in so doing to discourage in any way the healthy and beneficial devel-opmentof such companies.
As regards the exportation of electric power and gas, the key principle will be that quantities proposed to be exported must be surplus to present and reasonably foreseeable Canadian requirements.
In the case of electricity, it has been the policy in the past to grant only annual licences for export, so as to prevent permanent alienation of power. This remains our general policy, although some exceptions may be made in very special circumstances where the national interest would not be prejudiced by a longer term of export.
With regard to gas, we accept the recommendation of the Borden commission, which reads as follows:
Having regard to the proven reserves of natural gas in Canada and to trends in the discovery and growth of reserves, the export from Canada of natural gas, which may from time to time be surplus to the reasonably foreseeable requirements of Canada, be permitted under licence.
It appears necessary in granting licences for the export of gas to do so for periods up to 25 years in order to make possible the financing of the pipe line facilities.
Two governments must of course be agreed upon any such export. The first is the government of the province of origin. Until it declares gas available for removal from the province, this government can entertain no application for an export permit. After the province has declared gas surplus to its own requirements, the government of Canada, with the recommendation of the proposed national energy board, must decide whether it is also surplus to the requirements of Canada and, if so, upon what terms it may be exported, including the vital and complex question of price.

We are willing to work out an efficient arrangement with the United States which will satisfy our respective national requirements without hampering the mutually advantageous development of our gas industry. Our officials have already had discussions with appropriate officials of the United States state department and the federal power commission and we know from these talks that our willingness to co-operate and our desire to reach a flexible and mutually satisfactory working arrangement is reciprocated.
With regard to oil, it is not the intention at the present time to give authority in the bill for the issuing of export or import permits. However, a section of the bill will deal with this important matter and, if approved by parliament, will give authority to the governor in council to extend the application of the relevant portion of the bill to oil.
It will be evident, when the bill is distributed, that the experience of the past has been drawn upon extensively. Hon. members may wish to refer to Hansard of 1955, page 1523, for the debate on the Exportation of Power and Fluids and Importation of Gas Act. At that time the act of 1907 dealing with electricity was revised with particular reference to gas.
Hon. members may also read with profit the debate on the Pipe Lines Act of 1949, which is to be found at page 2509 of Hansard. The bill which is about to be introduced reproduces the substance of those two acts. Building on that foundation, we propose the setting up of a national energy board with appropriate powers to deal, so far as is within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, with the whole problem of the utilization of the abundant sources of electrical and petroleum energy in our country in the national interest.

importance of this new industry which has developed in Canada largely within the last few years.
Everyone is aware that we have moved into a new era in the development of sources of energy. The constantly increasing demands for electrical power have stimulated the use of most of the readily available sources of hydroelectric power. Thermal power units, based on the utilization of coal, are being constructed in increasing numbers. Rapid advance is being made in experiments leading to the harnessing of atomic power for the economic production of electricity. Side by side with these developments there has been a spectacular rise in the production and use of oil and gas and their byproducts, and an equally spectacular increase in the installation of pipe lines for the gathering, long distance transmission and distribution of oil and gas and their products.
Ten years ago when the hon. member for Laurier, then minister of transport, was speaking on this subject he estimated that the production of crude oil in Alberta was about 100,000 barrels per day; that after allowing for the prairie provinces' requirements of 60,000 barrels per day, there would be a surplus of 40,000 barrels for use elsewhere. He estimated total Canadian consumption at 290,000 barrels per day.
In 1959, ten years later, we find western Canadian crude oil production running at a rate of about 500,000 barrels per day, equivalent to roughly two-thirds of the total Canadian oil requirements. For the sixth year in a row, oil was Canada's leading mineral in 1959, its value of production exceeding $400 million. And though our oil exports suffered a setback in 1957-58, crude oil contributed $73 million to Canadian export income in the year 1958. This is an impressive figure when one considers that the export of crude oil to the United States began as recently as 1951, via the Interprovincial pipe line, and did not become substantial until 1955, the first full year of operation for the TransMountain pipe line.
Parallel developments have taken place in the natural gas industry. Proven reserves of natural gas in western Canada have increased from less than 5 trillion cubic feet in 1949 to more than 25 trillion cubic feet at the end of 1958. Net production of natural gas was 60 billion cubic feet in 1949; 336 billion in 1958. Further sharp increases can be expected to follow the recent construction of major pipe lines. Gas from northern Alberta and British Columbia started to flow to the Vancouver area and the Pacific northwestern states through the Westcoast pipe line in 1957, and the completion of the Trans-Canada pipe line in November, 1958
National Energy Board opened the markets of Ontario and the Montreal area to western Canadian gas.
Applications to export large quantities of gas to the western United States have now been approved by the government of Alberta, and related applications have been filed with this government and with the United States federal power commission. Other projects looking to exports to the United States middle west and to New York state are in preparation. One urgent reason why this government is anxious to press ahead with the measure referred to in the resolution before us is, of course, that we desire to establish with all proper speed administrative machinery for making appropriate disposition of such applications for gas export licences, in the light of government policy and in full consideration of all the interests involved.
The great and increasing growth in gas production and transmission industries has necessarily been accomplished by a remarkable development of the gas by-product industries. Some of the by-products, in particular sulphur, natural gasoline, propane and butane, are themselves valuable. Complicated and costly plants are required to remove them. There are now in Canada 22 such plants for the processing of natural gas and recovery of by-products.
Some export markets for propane and butane have already been developed. These markets were cut off in March when the United States oil import controls were made mandatory and extended to unfinished oil and products, but the exemption from new United States oil import controls announced on April 30 will restore access to such markets. There is good reason to hope that these natural gas liquids and sulphur will become increasingly important in our export trade.
All this growth in production, processing and transportation to market for oil and gas and related products has required an enormous quantity of capital. In 1949 about $90 million were invested in oil and gas exploration, production, processing, transportation and marketing facilities. For 1959 the comparable investment is estimated at $627 million, nearly 7 times as much, and some 13i per cent of total business capital expenditures planned for 1959 in Canada. In the decade ending in 1958 the cumulative totals were $4.4 billion, excluding land acquisition costs.
These figures cover only direct investment in petroleum expansion and do not take into account the secondary effects of investment in new industries based on petroleum, such
